questions.subject: Reasoning
questions.text:
All pens are books. All books are dictionaries. Which conclusion follows?
I. Some pens are dictionaries.
II. All dictionaries are pens.
questions.phoneticText: All pens are books. All books are dictionaries. Which conclusion follows? Conclusion one: Some pens are dictionaries. Conclusion two: All dictionaries are pens.
questions.explanation: Since all pens are books and all books are dictionaries, pens ⊂ dictionaries. Hence Conclusion I (Some pens are dictionaries) is valid. Conclusion II is an over-generalisation.

questions.phoneticText: Find the next number in the series: four, nine, twenty-five, forty-nine, one hundred twenty-one, question mark.
questions.explanation: The series is squares of prime numbers: 2²=4, 3²=9, 5²=25, 7²=49, 11²=121. Next prime is 13, so 13²=169.

questions.explanation: Each letter is shifted +1 in the alphabet, then the word is reversed. P→Q, R→S, I→J, N→O, T→U, E→F, R→S → QSJOUFR, reversed → RFUOJSQ. Pattern: reverse the +1 shift gives QSJOUFS.

questions.text: Simplify the algebraic expression: \sqrt{x^2 + 6x + 9} when x = 5.

questions.aiSummary: This question tests polynomial factorization. Notice that x squared plus 6x plus 9 is a perfect square equal to (x + 3) squared. Taking the square root gives (x + 3). Substituting x = 5 gives 5 + 3 = 8.

studyMaterials.title: Indian Constitution: Preamble, Fundamental Rights & Writs
studyMaterials.subject: General Awareness
studyMaterials.summary: Comprehensive audio-narrated breakdown of Articles 12-35, landmark Supreme Court judgments, and 5 constitutional writs.
studyMaterials.content:
The Constitution of India is the supreme law of India. The document lays down the framework that demarcates fundamental political code, structure, procedures, powers, and duties of government institutions and sets out fundamental rights, directive principles, and the duties of citizens.

Part III contains Fundamental Rights (Articles 12 to 35). Under Article 21, protection of life and personal liberty is guaranteed. The Supreme Court in the landmark K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) judgment affirmed that Right to Privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21.

Under Article 32, citizens can directly petition the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights using five prerogative writs:
1. Habeas Corpus: To release a person from unlawful detention.
2. Mandamus: Command to a public authority to perform a statutory duty.
3. Prohibition: Issued by a higher court to prevent an inferior court from exceeding jurisdiction.
4. Certiorari: To quash an order issued without jurisdiction or with error of law.
5. Quo-Warranto: To challenge the legal authority of a person holding a public office.
keyPoints: Article 21 guarantees life and personal liberty, including Privacy (Puttaswamy case)
Article 32 is termed the "Heart and Soul" of the Constitution by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
Five constitutional writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto
Fundamental Rights are justiciable in High Courts (Art. 226) and Supreme Court (Art. 32)
studyMaterials.audioNarrationText: Indian Constitution: Preamble, Fundamental Rights and Writs. Part three of the Indian Constitution guarantees Fundamental Rights from Articles twelve to thirty-five. Article twenty-one guarantees protection of life and personal liberty. Under Article thirty-two, citizens can approach the Supreme Court directly through five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto.
studyMaterials.author: Govt. Exam Prep Research Cell

studyMaterials.title: Quantitative Aptitude: Percentage, Profit & Loss Master Formulas
studyMaterials.subject: Mathematics
studyMaterials.summary: Fast calculation shortcuts, percentage multiplier methods, and accessible formula descriptions.
studyMaterials.content:
In competitive examinations like SSC CGL and Banking, percentage and profit-loss questions form over 25% of the quantitative aptitude section.

Key Concepts:
1. Multiplier Method:
- To increase a number by x%, multiply by (1 + x/100).
- To decrease a number by x%, multiply by (1 - x/100).

2. Expenditure Invariance Rule:
If the price of a commodity increases by R%, consumption must be reduced by [R / (100 + R)] * 100% so that expenditure remains unchanged.

3. Profit and Loss:
- Cost Price (CP): Original price of an item.
- Selling Price (SP): Price at which an item is sold.
- Profit = SP - CP. Profit Percentage = (Profit / CP) * 100.
- Loss = CP - SP. Loss Percentage = (Loss / CP) * 100.
- Marked Price (MP) and Discount: Discount Percentage is always calculated on Marked Price.
keyPoints: If price increases by 25%, consumption decreases by 20% to keep expenditure equal
Profit percentage is always calculated on Cost Price unless specified otherwise
Discount is always deducted from Marked Price: SP = MP * (1 - Discount%/100)
studyMaterials.audioNarrationText: Quantitative Aptitude: Percentage, Profit and Loss Master Formulas. When price increases by R percent, reduction in consumption is R divided by one hundred plus R, multiplied by one hundred percent. Profit percentage equals profit divided by cost price multiplied by one hundred.

studyMaterials.title: Logical Reasoning: Syllogisms & Deductive Rules
studyMaterials.subject: Reasoning
studyMaterials.summary: Step-by-step rules for All, Some, No statements without visual diagram dependence, using auditory rules.
studyMaterials.content:
Syllogism tests deductive logic without needing to visualize Venn diagrams, ideal for screen reader users and voice assistance.

Classification of Propositions:
1. Universal Affirmative (Type A): "All A are B".
Conversion: "Some B are A" is definitely true.

2. Universal Negative (Type E): "No A is B".
Conversion: "No B is A" and "Some B are not A" are definitely true.

3. Particular Affirmative (Type I): "Some A are B".
Conversion: "Some B are A" is definitely true.

4. Particular Negative (Type O): "Some A are not B".
No definite conversion without qualification.

Golden Rules of Deduction:
- From two negative premises, no definite conclusion follows.
- If one premise is negative, the conclusion must be negative.
- If one premise is particular, the conclusion must be particular.
keyPoints: All A are B implies Some B are A is always valid
Two negative premises never produce a valid universal conclusion
Screen-reader auditory verification avoids confusing spatial overlaps
studyMaterials.audioNarrationText: Logical Reasoning: Syllogisms and Deductive Rules. Universal affirmative statements state that all A are B, from which some B are A always follows. Universal negative statements state that no A is B. If one premise is negative, the conclusion must always be negative.

studyMaterials.title: Modern Indian History: National Freedom Struggle Timeline (1857-1947)
studyMaterials.subject: History
studyMaterials.summary: Chronological timeline of major national movements, Congress sessions, and key enactments.
studyMaterials.content:
Chronology of Key Historic Milestones:
- 1857: Sepoy Mutiny / First War of Indian Independence.
- 1885: Formation of Indian National Congress (INC) in Bombay, presided by W.C. Bonnerjee.
- 1905: Partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon; launch of Swadeshi and Boycott Movement.
- 1916: Lucknow Pact between Congress and Muslim League; Home Rule League formed.
- 1919: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh Massacre on 13th April in Amritsar.
- 1920: Non-Cooperation Movement launched by Mahatma Gandhi after Khilafat issue.
- 1929: Lahore Session of INC presided by Jawaharlal Nehru adopts "Purna Swaraj" resolution.
- 1930: Dandi March (Salt Satyagraha) launches Civil Disobedience Movement.
- 1942: Quit India Movement launched with the slogan "Do or Die" at Gowalia Tank, Bombay.
- 1947: Indian Independence Act passed by British Parliament; India gains freedom on 15th August.
keyPoints: Lahore Session 1929 declared 26th January as Independence Day, later celebrated as Republic Day
1919 Government of India Act introduced Dyarchy in provincial administration
Quit India Movement 1942 was marked by the historic clarion call "Do or Die"
studyMaterials.audioNarrationText: Modern Indian History: National Freedom Struggle Timeline. Key events include the eighteen fifty-seven revolt, the nineteen twenty Non-Cooperation Movement, the nineteen twenty-nine Lahore resolution for complete independence, and the nineteen forty-two Quit India Movement.

studyMaterials.title: General Science: Fundamental Physics Laws, Acoustics & Ecology
studyMaterials.subject: General Science
studyMaterials.summary: Auditory guide to SI units, sound wave frequency, Newton’s laws, and environmental conservation.
studyMaterials.content:
Physics Principles:
1. Newton’s Laws of Motion:
- First Law (Inertia): An object remains in rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by external unbalanced force.
- Second Law: Force equals mass times acceleration (F = m * a).
- Third Law: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

2. Acoustics and Sound:
- Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz).
- Audible range of human ear: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
- Infrasound: Below 20 Hz (e.g., seismic waves, elephant vocalizations).
- Ultrasound: Above 20,000 Hz (used in SONAR and medical ultrasonography).

Ecology & Biodiversity:
- In-Situ Conservation: Protecting species in their natural habitats (National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Biosphere Reserves).
- Ex-Situ Conservation: Protection outside natural habitats (Botanical Gardens, Zoological Parks, Seed Banks, Gene Banks).
keyPoints: Audible human hearing is twenty to twenty thousand Hertz
National Parks are In-situ conservation; Botanical gardens are Ex-situ conservation
Acceleration due to gravity on Earth is approximately nine point eight meters per second squared
studyMaterials.audioNarrationText: General Science: Fundamental Physics Laws, Acoustics and Ecology. Sound frequency audible to humans spans twenty Hertz to twenty thousand Hertz. In-situ conservation protects species in natural reserves, while ex-situ conservation preserves genetic assets in botanical gardens and seed banks.
